name: architecture-standards-init-example
oneLiner: What the architectural constitution produces when pointed at an empty repository — compliant on the first commit, not after a later cleanup pass.
summary: A worked run of the greenfield initializer: one Aspire composition root, one shared kernel, one service that owns its database, one Next.js surface in front of it, three Fly.io apps and eight workflows. It **ships no domain model, deliberately** — it exists to be read as an example of the architecture, not used as a product. This is the most important companion piece to `architecture-standards`: the constitution describes what a system should look like, and this repository shows that shape without a single line of domain to distract from it. Several things here are done better than in most real systems: the frontend reads its configuration per request from `/api/config` and never from `NEXT_PUBLIC_*`, because that bakes at build time and costs one image per environment; the shared kernel is 477 lines against an 800-line ceiling enforced by a test **and** a CI step; and the setup script **generates** the one mandatory secret, because a human asked to invent one produces `changeme`.
tests: Nine test attributes in `tests/…Api.Tests` (the README says ten tests): the zero-credential health report, list clamping, the error shape and three kernel guards. Alongside them, four Playwright tests through the whole stack, run on every pull request — and those are the strong point here, because they boot exactly the Docker-less path the repository advertises.
ci: Eight workflows — the most of any repository added in this pass: `ci.yml` with the E2E suite, `codeql.yml`, `secret-scan.yml`, `pages.yml`, `build-overview-pdf.yml`, and three Fly.io workflows (deploy, scale, and a teardown gated by a typed confirmation).

docs.label: The setup script — it generates the secret rather than asking for one

components.name: The Aspire composition root
components.description: Declares Postgres, the API and the frontend with `WithReference`, `WaitFor` and `WithHttpHealthCheck`. Explicitly **not** the production topology — and the repository says so outright, which is the most commonly confused point about Aspire.

components.name: The shared kernel
components.description: Telemetry, health, discovery, resilience, JWT, CORS, OpenAPI, the database provider — 477 lines. An architecture test asserts the kernel holds no entity type and exports nothing you can inherit from.

components.name: The product surface
components.description: The browser's only origin. Its server side reads configuration per request from `/api/config` and reaches the API through a catch-all proxy that walks a candidate ladder — one code path works on a laptop, under Aspire and on Fly.

components.name: The setup scripts
components.description: Check prerequisites, restore both dependency graphs, and **generate** the one mandatory secret into `dotnet user-secrets`. `--check` reports what is missing and changes nothing. The PowerShell variant does the same job without `openssl`, which is not a command on Windows.

components.name: The E2E suite
components.description: Four Playwright tests through the whole stack, booting the Docker-less path on every pull request. That is not a convenience — it is principle P8 turned into something checkable.

overlaps.reason: This is that initializer's output and the one complete worked example of the constitution with no domain to distract. A change to the standard that cannot be reproduced here is a standard nobody has executed.

The same skeleton reached from the other side: a 2018 solution modernized there, greenfield here. The kernel with its line ceiling, the in-memory database fallback and post-Kestrel migrations are identical in both.
The kernel carries the JWT wiring but the issuer is external — the same split as everywhere in this portfolio: a service validates tokens and cannot mint them.

product: Credibility, not a transaction, and the highest value-to-size ratio in cluster B. For a consulting buyer it answers the question 'what does your first commit look like': not a slide, but a repository that boots with no credential and carries eight gates from day one. What sells here is the initialization method, not the code.
highlights: Configuration read per request from `/api/config` instead of `NEXT_PUBLIC_*`. That is the mistake most Next.js deployments make, and it costs one image per environment — here it is solved in the skeleton before anyone has a chance to make it.

The setup script generates the secret instead of asking a human to invent one. The justification recorded in the repository is one sentence and it is correct: a human asked to invent a secret produces `changeme`.

The kernel ceiling is enforced by two independent mechanisms — an architecture test and a CI step. The duplication is deliberate: the test protects in the editor, the CI step protects against a test somebody deleted.
The dependency count per project is printed in the README. A rise in a diff becomes a question somebody can ask at review — a cheap mechanism with a disproportionate effect.
gaps: Five open Dependabot pull requests against zero open issues — every open item in this repository is a dependency update.

Shipping no domain model is a decision, but it has a price: the repository cannot show how the constitution copes with a domain that does not fit in one service. The hardest architectural question stays untouched here.
Nine test attributes on the API side is thin for a repository that advertises its gates — the burden of proof rests on four E2E tests.
next: Merge the five Dependabot pull requests. With zero issues open, it is the only outstanding work in this repository.
Add a second service to the example, or record as an explicit decision that one service is the limit of what the initializer demonstrates.
Wire this example into `architecture-standards`' validation: a change to the constitution that cannot be reproduced here should fail that repository's build.
risks: The example is compliant with the constitution as of the day it was generated. Without a gate binding it to the standard it will drift silently — and that would be the worst possible kind of drift, because this repository is cited as the reference shape.
headline: Eight workflows, zero credentials needed to run it, zero domain — exactly as designed
